assets.topic: Disentangling media taste from violent intent (the James Vance pattern)
assets.visual_frame_description: A high-school counseling office in Fresno. Guidance counselor Maya Okada sits at a desk with three-dozen-year-old headphones beside a laptop, reviewing the file of Derek, a 17-year-old whose friend reported him saying his favorite band could order him to do anything. On the monitor is a journal page covered in rewritten song lyrics, and behind the desk a wall poster reads 'Listen: the first survival skill.'
assets.player_mission: Scan Derek's media file and pick the single observation that best flags a violence-prone pattern rather than ordinary musical taste. You must distinguish what the evidence actually shows from what panicked adults usually blame.
key_concepts: In the Vance case, de Becker could not show that the Judas Priest album Stained Class compelled the shootings; the court decided the record store could not have predicted them.
James Vance rewrote a lyric about a child being cared for ('fed him by hand') into a cannibalistic image ('fed him a hand'), showing violence was projected onto the music rather than created by it.
James Vance said the band did not need to command him: if they had said 'let's see who can kill the most people,' he would have gone out and done something terrible.

De Becker's hypothetical list of the hundred most significant influences (PINs) preceding teen violence places an addiction to media products somewhere on the list, with alcohol and drugs closer to the top.
Alcohol and drugs are proven and intended to affect the perceptions and behavior of everyone who ingests them, unlike media products.
A fascination with violence and guns was a central part of James's personality, to the point of planning to become a gunsmith and playing 'war' as 'training to be a mercenary.'
James and Ray were not despondent the night of the shooting; they were wild, high on drugs and alcohol, and had considered a shooting spree at a nearby shopping center.
The grisly imagery that disturbed adults was 'fairly mundane' to James because he had been getting comfortable with graphic violence for a long while.
A man killed while listening to an Ozzy Osbourne tape on headphones had actually been struck by a train; a colleague joked he was 'killed by heavy metal, literally.'

When James was asked what else could have caused the shootings, he answered sarcastically 'a bad relationship? The stars being right? The tide being out?', which is as reasonable as blaming lyrics once family life is excluded.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests attribution bias in media-violence debates: observers displace causation onto a product (the band, the album) while the PINs documented in the case pointed to drugs, alcohol, gun fascination, and chronic feelings of being ignored. De Becker argues the violence predates and shapes the media interest, so the strongest cue is the respondent's active rewriting and weaponizing of content, not the content itself.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.target_channel: A teenager's media consumption and stated relationship to violent content
assets.question: Derek's file contains several media-related observations. Which single observation is the strongest warning signal of violence-proneness rather than ordinary musical taste?
assets.correct_cue: Derek rewrote a lyric that describes a child being fed and cared for into an image of cannibalism, telling his friend the band could make him do anything, even kill. This mirrors James Vance, who changed 'they bathed him and clothed him and fed him by hand' into 'fed him a hand' and insisted he would do anything for the band, including killing people. The rewriting shows the violence was already inside the listener and is being projected onto the media, whereas the album's gore being passively consumed is the detail de Becker found mundane; the case record shows the shootings happened with alcohol, drugs, and a fascination with guns as the PINs closest to the top of his hypothetical list of a hundred influences.
distractors: Derek exclusively listens to a heavy-metal band whose album covers show demons and gore.
Derek owns several hundred music albums and plays them loudly late at night.
Derek reads internet fan forums about the band and wears its concert shirt to school.
assets.underlying_psychology: This is externalization and attribution error: families sued the band because blaming a product is easier than examining parenting, family life, and the child's own choices. De Becker notes that by pointing at the band, James 'washed away all of the scrutiny that might reasonably have been focused on himself, his family, or even his society,' and the same displacement pattern is what makes the rewriting cue the diagnostic one.

assets.topic: Parricide pre-incident indicators (child abuse as the reliable PIN)
assets.visual_frame_description: A dim interview room in an Albuquerque police station. Detective Lena Ruiz sits across from Tyler, a 14-year-old who was brought in after a teacher found bruises and a journal entry. Between them on the table are school nurse reports and a child protective services intake form, and through the one-way glass a victim advocate watches the boy press his palms flat on the table as he talks.
assets.player_mission: Study Tyler's history and identify which detail is the most reliable pre-incident indicator of parricide risk according to the evidence Paul Mones assembled. Choose the cue that prediction research actually supports, not the one that merely feels alarming.
key_concepts: Paul Mones, author of When a Child Kills, observes that for parricide, events occurring twelve years before the killing are as important as events occurring twelve hours before it.
The single most reliable pre-incident indicator of parricide is child abuse.
Children who kill their parents are usually found to have been beaten, degraded, sodomized, tied up, or tortured in other ways.
Mike, a sixteen-year-old parricide defendant, had been beaten by his father from kindergarten on and carried constant injuries attributed to 'falling off his bike,' 'tripping,' or 'cutting himself.'
Mike's father eventually held a pistol out to him and said, 'You got two choices: you kill me or I kill you.'
Most runaway children leave home to escape abuse or to call attention to it; Mones says children who stay 'lay family secrets bare with the report of a gun.'
Adult victims of rape or hijacking are often as docile under attack as children, so a child's passivity during abuse is not evidence against the abuse.
A boy named Robbie shot and killed his drunken father at age three after watching his mother being beaten, and gunpowder tests confirmed he had fired the gun.
Robbie explained his act matter-of-factly: 'I killed him. Now he's dead. If he would have hit my mother again, I would have shot him again.'
Parricide and other awful violence inside a family leaves warning signs that must be reported by parents, teachers, policemen, neighbors, and relatives, not by the children themselves.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests pre-incident indicator reasoning for intrafamily violence: the single most reliable PIN for parricide is a documented history of child abuse, and the predictive window is years, not hours. De Becker, following Mones, stresses that abuse visible in medical records and family patterns is the signal to act on, while surface provocations are noise.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.target_channel: Family history and injury patterns reported by a teenager in crisis
assets.question: Tyler's file shows several details. Which one is the most reliable pre-incident indicator of parricide per the evidence de Becker presents?
assets.correct_cue: Tyler's school nurse log documents repeated injuries over years, each attributed by the family to 'falling off his bike,' 'tripping,' and 'cutting himself,' alongside a pattern of discipline that involves beatings that began when he entered kindergarten. This is the child-abuse signature Mones identifies as the single most reliable pre-incident indicator of parricide, the same signature visible in Mike's case where a jury later saw the scars his father gave him. The abuse history matters even if it began twelve years before any possible crisis, because in parricide prediction the long view is as important as the recent view.
distractors: Tyler's grades dropped sharply during the last month of the school term.
Tyler recently started watching action movies with violent fight scenes.
Tyler's mother works a night shift and is rarely home during the week.
assets.underlying_psychology: The mechanism is chronic, escalating family trauma rather than sudden provocation: de Becker and Mones show that parricides emerge from years of abuse in which the child is the docile victim, mirroring how even adults submit passively during rape or hijacking. Distractors such as recent grades or media habits are temporally close but causally weak, while the years-long abuse pattern is the PIN the book's evidence actually supports.

assets.topic: Institutional denial: the school that predicted Joey's offense and ignored it
assets.visual_frame_description: A suburban elementary school office in Houston. Parent activist Marcus Grand spreads photocopied documents across a conference table: a transfer file, an arrest report, and a district policy book. A framed district motto on the wall reads 'Every Child, Every Day,' and through the window two security guards in untucked shirts stand chatting near the playground without looking at the children.
assets.player_mission: Compare the documents against the district's claims and identify which element proves the school was making high-stakes predictions while choosing denial. Your choice determines whether a pattern of negligent supervision is visible in the record.
key_concepts: Schools are in the business of high-stakes predictions, regularly facing questions like whether a visitor will kidnap a child or whether a student will bring a lethal weapon to school.
The offender de Becker calls Joey, a grammar school student, sodomized a seven-year-old boy in the school bathroom.
A month before the rape, Joey had been arrested for victimizing another boy the same way in the same bathroom.
Joey's previous school had predicted in writing that he would act out in sexually inappropriate ways and sent his records to the school where the rapes occurred.
The school district had maintained a specific written policy titled 'Child-On-Child Sexual Abuse' for years, proving such events were foreseen as a class of risk.

Joey wore warning signs 'like a banner': carrying a knife, threatening homicide, threatening and attempting suicide, lighting a building on fire, pouring gasoline on his mother, and displaying aggression and inappropriate sexual conduct toward other children.
The principal did not tell Joey's teachers about the first rape accusation, so no one could increase supervision.
When one teacher found Joey unmanageable, he was moved to a class of younger, smaller boys, which de Becker likens to providing a 'beauty contest' of victims.
The principal arranged for Joey to be escorted to the bathroom not by an adult but by another student.

Hiring guards is a typical response to pressure on organizations, but guards without training, supervision, an intelligent plan, or basic information can hurt more than help because everyone stops looking at safety.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests organizational denial at the prediction stage: the school possessed written predictions and a formal child-on-child abuse policy, yet administrators responded with information suppression and victim-adjacent placements. De Becker frames the failure as individual and organizational laziness plus the hope that a problem will 'go away' if ignored, which is why the documented prediction, not the absence of policy, is the decisive cue.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.target_channel: Written school records and administrative responses to a student's escalation
assets.question: The district claimed the rape could not have been predicted. Which element of the record most clearly disproves that claim and shows the school chose denial?
assets.correct_cue: The transfer file contains a written prediction from Joey's prior school that he would act out in sexually inappropriate ways, and the police report shows he was arrested one month earlier for victimizing another boy the same way in the same bathroom. De Becker emphasizes these documented artifacts: the previous school predicted the exact behavior in writing, and the 'Child-On-Child Sexual Abuse' policy on the district's books proves the administration knew the risk class existed. Against that record, the principal's choices (withholding the information from teachers, moving Joey into a class of younger and smaller boys, assigning a student escort) show the warning signs were known and then ignored.
distractors: The school district had no written policy at all about child-on-child sexual abuse.
The school employed no security guards on its campus at the time of the offense.
Joey's standardized test scores placed him below grade level in reading.
assets.underlying_psychology: The mechanism is motivated denial inside a prediction system: de Becker notes the school's own written policy 'in effect raises a predictive question for every principal,' and Joey's behavior answered it, standing up in the imaginary assembly while the principal turned away. The presence of effective procedures would have been the protective factor; instead the record shows security theater, untrained guards, and hope that the problem would disappear, which is precisely the negligence pattern the book documents.

assets.topic: Sibling-age violence: pre-teens who kill within the family
assets.visual_frame_description: A kitchen table in Charlotte, North Carolina, after dinner. Nora and Phil Blanchard sit across from family therapist Dana Whitfield; their 10-year-old son Eric is upstairs. On the table are a pediatrician's notes about their 6-year-old daughter's bruises and a calendar where Mrs. Blanchard has circled the dates of three 'accidents,' while a baby monitor crackles softly between them.
assets.player_mission: Review the parents' descriptions of Eric's behavior toward his little sister and choose the detail that should be treated as a genuine warning, not dismissed as sibling rivalry. Identify the pattern de Becker says families fatally underestimate.
key_concepts: Unlike teens, pre-teens who kill within the family are more likely to kill a sibling than a parent.
De Becker notes such violence does not happen without warning, and most cases have involved an abused or severely disturbed child whose prior attempts to kill a sibling were not taken seriously.
Many people believe violence by children against children is a natural part of growing up, a belief de Becker challenges directly.
When a child does something that places another child in serious hazard, it should not be ignored, whatever its frequency in sibling life.
The school in Joey's case ignored clear warning signs because administrators treated child-on-child harm as unpredicted despite decades of policy and a prior arrest.
Federal research followed 1,600 children who had been abused or neglected for nearly twenty years, and fully half of them had been arrested for some crime.
Children are often seen as burdens to society, but they are in fact the primary child-care providers in America, caring for siblings, the elderly, and themselves.
The warning signs of violence between children are shown to parents, teachers, policemen, neighbors, and relatives, and adults must report them.
Of all the violence discussed in the book, being killed by one's own child is the easiest to avoid, and a virtually guaranteed precaution starts years early: being a loving parent.
Escalation of force toward a sibling should raise the question of abuse or disturbance in the offender's own background, since most such cases involve an abused or severely disturbed child.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests minimization bias in family settings: adults routinely classify child-on-child violence as normal growing-up behavior even when it places another child in serious hazard. De Becker counters that pre-teen family killers almost always had prior attempts on a sibling that went unheeded, so the duration, secrecy, and force of the pattern are the cues that separate play from pre-incident indicator.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.target_channel: Parent-reported sibling interactions and injury explanations
assets.question: Mrs. Blanchard lists several things Eric does to his sister. Which single reported detail should be treated as a serious warning rather than dismissed as rivalry between children?
assets.correct_cue: Eric has twice held a pillow over his younger sister's face until she struggled, and last month, out of view of the adults, he pushed her head under the bathwater until an older cousin intervened. De Becker's evidence shows pre-teen family killers usually made earlier attempts on a sibling that were not taken seriously because adults believed child-on-child violence was a natural part of growing up; a repeated, concealed, force-escalating act that places another child in serious hazard is precisely the pattern that must not be ignored. The secretiveness and the targeting of a smaller, more vulnerable child distinguish it from ordinary disagreements.
distractors: Eric and his sister argue loudly over toys at least twice a day.
Eric sometimes takes his sister's dessert before she finishes dinner.
Eric once pushed his sister during a backyard game of tag and she scraped her knee.
assets.underlying_psychology: The mechanism is normalization of child-on-child hazard: de Becker notes that because many people believe such violence is part of growing up, prior attempts at serious harm go unrecorded and untreated until tragedy. Cross-referencing the book's finding that most such offenders are themselves abused or severely disturbed, and that half of abused or neglected children in a long-term federal study were later arrested, the correct response to a concealed, escalating attempt is protective intervention rather than minimization.

assets.topic: Attention-getting violence: the 'ignored for 20 years' PIN
assets.visual_frame_description: A windowless youth-services office in Detroit at six in the evening. Counselor Terrence Wu transcribes notes from his third session with Devon, a 19-year-old who has been writing elaborate letters to a famous singer about being invisible. A corkboard behind Wu holds photographs of news clippings about attention-seeking crimes, and Devon's letter lies open on the desk with the phrase 'you will finally see me' underlined three times.
assets.player_mission: Read Devon's statements and choose the one that matches the leading pre-incident indicator de Becker identifies for attention-getting violent acts. Distinguish a need for recognition from ordinary frustration.
key_concepts: James Vance said he felt 'ignored for 20 years,' which de Becker calls one of the leading PINs for attention-getting violent acts.
James perceived the Judas Priest song 'Hero's End' to be about how one has to die to be recognized.
In the lives of too many teenagers, recognition is more meaningful than accomplishment, and as it was for James, recognition can be available through violence.
With the pull of a trigger, a young person whose upbringing has not invested him with self-worth can become significant and 'un-ignorable.'
De Becker studied fifty-six other cases involving young people who connected a music star to their violent acts, suicides, or suicide threats.
One teenager asked a famous singer to send him a gun to commit suicide; another threatened suicide unless a female recording artist visited him.
A man who believed a female recording artist was his wife and was hiding from him attempted suicide by cutting his wrists.
Another wrote that 'when I attempt suicide it won't be an attempt,' framing the act as a guaranteed spectacle.
The 200,000 acts of violence a child will witness in media by age 18 are learned by modeling and imitation, a concern author David Walsh likens to 'a guest in our families that advocates violence.'
Without perseverance or self-discipline, and with expectations of the world that change day to day, recognition through violence can seem the only path to significance.
assets.theory_summary: This scenario tests the attention-seeking driver behind a class of violent acts: chronic invisibility converts into a plan to become significant and 'un-ignorable,' often staged so the recognition is guaranteed. De Becker's PIN is the stated experience of being ignored for years coupled with the belief that recognition demands an extreme act, as with James's reading of 'Hero's End' as dying to be seen.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.target_channel: A disaffected young person's statements about recognition and visibility
assets.question: Devon makes several statements across his sessions. Which one matches the leading PIN de Becker identifies for attention-getting violent acts?
assets.correct_cue: Devon says, 'Nobody has really seen me since I was a kid, and the only way anyone finally looks at you is if you do something no one can ignore,' and he has started drafting letters to a recording artist describing how he could make himself impossible to overlook. This mirrors James Vance's 'ignored for 20 years' admission and his reading of 'Hero's End' as a song about dying to be recognized. De Becker identifies chronic felt invisibility as one of the leading PINs for attention-getting violence because for undervalued young people recognition outweighs accomplishment, and the trigger pull offers instant significance and 'un-ignorability.'
distractors: Devon complains that his entry-level job does not pay enough to cover rent.
Devon says he argues with his girlfriend about how much time she spends with her friends.
Devon mentions that he has no interest in the music charts and rarely watches television.
assets.underlying_psychology: The mechanism is violated significance needs: when self-worth was never invested by upbringing, violence becomes a vehicle for recognition, and the fantastical bond with a remote star (James called the band 'metal gods' and described the relationship as a marriage 'until death do us part') supplies an audience that real life never did. De Becker counts feeling ignored among the leading PINs, and the fifty-six star-involved cases he examined show the recurring shape of acts designed to guarantee that someone, finally, looks.

assets.topic: The blame-shifting audit: a parent's media allegation
assets.visual_frame_description: A deposition room in Dayton, Ohio, with a court reporter at a stenotype machine. Leticia Moran, a 46-year-old accountant whose son joined a suicide pact after months of drinking, sits across from a lawyer from the record store's defense. Boxes of album liner notes and sales receipts line the table, and sunlight from a tall window crosses her hands as she grips a copy of the album cover.
assets.player_mission: Audit Mrs. Moran's account of causation and determine whether her accusation against the record store is a reliable explanation. Weigh her stated beliefs against the documented behavior of her son.
key_concepts: James Vance's mother blamed the heavy-metal band Judas Priest and the record store that sold their records for her son's suicide pact.
She insisted the proprietors should have predicted that the album Stained Class would compel her son, and that the store should have warned the boys about the album's 'lethality.'

Researchers in de Becker's office found one man who became sick after ingesting a vinyl record, another who had a heart attack dancing to polka music, and another who made a weapon from shards of a broken record.
The range of things people might do with any product makes it next to impossible to foresee all risks.
De Becker's hypothetical list of the hundred most significant influences preceding teen violence puts alcohol and drugs above media addiction.
James and Ray were high on drugs and alcohol on the night of the shooting and had destroyed Ray's room before running through the streets with the shotgun.
James said of an acquaintance who attempted suicide repeatedly that drug problems 'go hand in hand,' and he called alcoholics violent from his own life experience.
By pointing his trigger finger at a rock band, James washed away scrutiny that might reasonably have been focused on himself, his family, or his society.
The court decided the proprietors of the record store could not have predicted the shootings.
Families cannot sue Satan or Allah, so record stores and musical groups are sometimes all they have left to blame.
assets.theory_summary: This audit tests external attribution in grief: a grieving parent locates causation in a product because it is suable and concrete, while the documented PINs (alcohol, drugs, gun fascination, felt invisibility) point elsewhere. De Becker's casework found media products could not be shown to compel violence, which is why the accusation, however sincerely delivered, is not a reliable causal explanation.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.question: Is Mrs. Moran's claim that the album and its seller caused her son's and his friend's actions a reliable causal explanation?
assets.subject_baseline: Mrs. Moran is a precise, church-going accountant whose neighbors describe her as composed and organized. In the two years before her son's hospitalization, she kept meticulous scrapbooks of his activities and, by her own account, rarely knew which friends he was with or what he drank, because 'boys will be boys.' She is articulate in meetings and normally defers politely to figures of authority.
assets.observed_nonverbal_log: 09:42 Audit begins; Mrs. Moran enters with the album cover held flat against her chest like a document she expects to file. 09:51 When asked about her son's drinking, she smooths the album sleeve and answers 'That has nothing to do with the music question.' 10:05 Describing the album artwork to the lawyer, her voice becomes firm and her index finger taps the demonic image rapidly. 10:14 Asked about a time her son came home intoxicated, she looks at the ceiling, pauses four seconds, and says 'I don't recall that night.' 10:26 When the lawyer reads her own letter calling the album 'lethal,' she nods forcefully and repeats the word 'lethal' twice. 10:38 Asked to describe her son's friends, she straightens her back and says 'The boys he ran with were not from our side of town.'
assets.interrogation_transcript:
Defense counsel: 'You believe the store should have known this album would lead to what happened?'
Mrs. Moran: 'They sold it to him. They should have warned us about the lethality of that record.'
Defense counsel: 'Did your son drink alcohol or use drugs in the months before?'
Mrs. Moran: 'Boys experiment. That has nothing to do with the music question.'
Defense counsel: 'You wrote to the store that the album compelled your son.'
Mrs. Moran: 'Yes. Every night he listened to it, and it put thoughts into him.'
Defense counsel: 'What did he say about the band?'
Mrs. Moran: 'He called them metal gods. He said they were his bible.'
Defense counsel: 'Did he ever mention feeling ignored at home?'
Mrs. Moran: 'He was loved. Very loved. I don't think we need to go into our home.'
assets.correct_diagnosis: The accusation is sincere but diagnostically unreliable: it is grief-driven external attribution, not causation. The album was present in the boy's life, but de Becker's casework found no shown mechanism by which a recording compels violence, and the court in the analogous Vance case ruled the store could not have predicted the shootings. The reliable PINs in the boy's own record were alcohol and drug use (which de Becker places near the top of the influence list, above media addiction), a fascination with violence and guns, and stated feelings of being ignored, all of which Mrs. Moran deflects or cannot recall.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: Evidence vs. verdict: (1) The mother's 'lethality' claim rests on lyrics and artwork, but de Becker's research team documented bizarre behaviors tied to many products (eating vinyl, weaponizing record shards), showing product risk cannot be foreseen from content alone. (2) Her own testimony confirms heavy drinking and experiments with drugs in the year before, matching James's description of alcoholics as violent and his report that drug problems and suicidality 'go hand in hand.' (3) She deflects questions about family life and her son's friendship circle, the very domains de Becker says the band-blame 'washed away' from scrutiny. (4) Facts the mother does not dispute make the record store's lack of prediction reasonable: the range of things any consumer might do with a product is unforeseeable. Verdict: the explanation is an externalizing attribution that relocates cause onto a suable product; the pre-incident indicators that actually preceded the violence lay in substance use, violence fascination, and invisibility.
distractors: The album's lyrics demonstrably compel violent behavior in listeners, as shown by studies of subliminal messages.
The store's legal duty to warn customers about album content means its failure is the true cause of the tragedy.
The son's actions were caused by a diagnosable mental illness that made prediction impossible for any party.

assets.topic: The forthcoming teen: Marcus Dane and the Massey pattern
assets.visual_frame_description: A juvenile detention interview room with a metal table bolted to the floor. Sixteen-year-old Marcus Dane sits forward, smiling, across from forensic interviewer Irina Petrov, who has reviewed school reports of animal cruelty that children in his neighborhood described. A stack of confiscated sketchbooks sits beside her, filled with drawings of skulls and one figure labeled 'the girls I will find.'
assets.player_mission: Determine whether Marcus's interview reveals documented pre-incident indicators of violence or merely teenage edginess. Decide what the evidence supports about his risk and about the adults who had contact with him.
key_concepts: Jason Massey, who killed a fourteen-year-old boy and his thirteen-year-old step-sister, idolized serial killers Ted Bundy and Henry Lee Lucas and avidly followed the music group Slayer.
In the years before he killed, Massey slaughtered cows, cats, and dogs and kept the skulls.
Massey spoke often of wanting to kill girls, robbed a fast-food restaurant, and stalked and terrorized a teenage girl for five years with letters about slitting her throat and drinking her blood.
So many details of Massey's behavior were known to people around him, 'and yet denial prevailed.'

Daniel Goleman's Emotional Intelligence lists seven key abilities most beneficial for humans: to motivate ourselves, to persist against frustration, to delay gratification, to regulate moods, to hope, to empathize, and to control impulse.
Many who commit violence never learned those abilities; knowing a young person who lacks them all is an important pre-incident indicator, and chronic anger in childhood is another predictor.
A lack of impulse control likely explains the gruesome things Massey did, such as cutting off the girl's hands and head.
Massey was forthcoming about his goals: 'All I want is the murdering of countless young women. I wish to reap sorrow for the families.'
Anger of this kind at family does not come out of nowhere.

Juvenile murder is relatively rare, but about one in five people killed by teenagers is a stranger killed during a robbery, and 75 percent of homicides by young people occur when they are high or drunk.
assets.theory_summary: This audit tests the willingness to credit a young person's documented pattern over his polished presentation: cruelty to animals, idolization of killers, stated homicidal wishes, and missing impulse control are the PINs, while articulateness and good manners are presentation, not evidence. De Becker's recurring finding is that the signs were known and 'yet denial prevailed,' so the audit's verdict rests on the chronic, escalating evidence trail rather than the interview manner.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.question: Does Marcus Dane's interview reveal documented pre-incident indicators of violence, or is his behavior explainable teenage edginess within normal bounds?
assets.subject_baseline: Marcus is articulate, reads above grade level, and is described by his grandmother as affectionate and polite with her. Neighbors describe a boy who is uncommonly quiet at the park, and his school counselor notes he never shows anger in class. The family has no police complaints against him apart from reports this year from parents whose pets have disappeared.
assets.observed_nonverbal_log: 11:05 Interview begins; Marcus shakes hands firmly and asks the interviewer to call him Marc. 11:12 Asked about his weekend, he describes trapping a squirrel in vivid detail, smiling with his teeth visible as he narrates. 11:20 When shown a confiscated drawing of a skull, he leans in, traces the jawline with his finger, and nods approvingly. 11:31 Asked what he thinks his neighbors feel about the missing pets, his face goes flat; he shrugs and says 'probably nothing.' 11:44 He volunteers that his favorite biography is about Ted Bundy, and his eyes brighten while his tone stays conversational. 11:58 Asked about his future, he says 'All I want is the murdering of countless young women. I wish to reap sorrow for the families,' then laughs and calls it a joke from a song.
assets.interrogation_transcript:
Interviewer: 'Tell me about the drawings in your sketchbook.'
Marcus: 'The skulls are my favorite thing to draw. I keep them real.'
Interviewer: 'Real?'
Marcus: 'Real bones. I have a collection under the porch. The cats were hardest to catch.'
Interviewer: 'What happened to the cats?'
Marcus: 'Same thing that happens to everything. I'm very careful, so nobody knows what happened.'
Interviewer: 'Who do you admire?'
Marcus: 'Ted Bundy was smart. He got away with it for years because people trusted him, like they trust me.'
Interviewer: 'And you said you want to reap sorrow for families?'
Marcus: 'That's what I want. But it was a joke from a song, you know, like the others in my family don't know anything.'
assets.correct_diagnosis: The interview reveals documented pre-incident indicators of violence that demand intervention. Marcus matches the Massey pattern element by element: escalating cruelty to animals with retained trophies (skulls under the porch), explicit admiration of a serial killer he says he resembles in trustworthiness, and a stated homicidal wish delivered with flat affect, all presented inside a polite, articulate package. Goleman's framework applies: Marcus shows no capacity for empathy or impulse control in the interview, and chronic cruelty is itself a recognized predictor. As in Massey's case the neighbors, counselor, and family hold individual details, and de Becker's lesson is that denial prevailed there too; the correct verdict is that the boy is a documented risk requiring immediate professional help and supervision, not a diagnosis of mere edginess.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: Evidence vs. verdict: (1) Escalation pattern: Marcus progressed from behaviors 'nobody knows about' to narrated cruelty and retained skulls, matching the animal-cruelty escalation de Becker documents in Massey's years before murder. (2) Identification pattern: admiration of Ted Bundy and a claim of manipulative trustworthiness echo Massey's idolization of Bundy and Lucas, which was among the obvious warning signs people ignored. (3) Stated intent: the 'countless young women' statement is nearly verbatim Massey's confession of goals, and the 'it was a joke' recovery demonstrates exactly the presentation problem de Becker warns about, since criminals can sound like anyone. (4) Empathy and impulse deficits: flat affect when discussing neighbors' losses and vivid animation when describing cruelty indicate missing Goleman abilities; 'knowing a young person who lacks them all... is an important pre-incident indicator.' Verdict: the evidence trail is chronic, escalating, and documented; the risk verdict must follow the PINs, not the performance.
distractors: Marcus's good grades and articulate manner prove the reports are exaggerations by neighborhood children.
Cruelty to animals is common among boys Marcus's age and has no documented relationship to later violence toward people.

assets.topic: The three-year-old's testimony: Robbie's account of killing his father

A one-way mirror reflects the tinted glass behind him.

The father was drunk and had left a gun on the table.

Paul Mones observes that the single most reliable pre-incident indicator of parricide is child abuse.
Children who kill their parents are usually found to have been beaten, degraded, sodomized, tied up, or tortured in other ways.

Adult victims of rape or hijacking are often as docile as children, and we do not blame them afterward for failing to act.

De Becker and Mones show the gun report 'lays family secrets bare,' making the child's calm account evidence of a protective motive learned in terror, not of callousness.

assets.question: What does three-year-old Robbie's account of killing his father actually diagnose about the dynamics of this family violence?
assets.subject_baseline: Robbie's pediatrician describes a small, developmentally ordinary three-year-old who is shy with new adults and clingy with his mother. Neighbors report the father drinking heavily on weekends and loud, breaking sounds coming from the apartment. Robbie's mother appears in the file as petite, soft-spoken, and repeatedly photographed with fresh bruises, each explained as falls or kitchen accidents.

I got the gun. I shot him.' Interviewer: 'Can you tell me what happened that night?'
Robbie: 'Daddy was hitting Mommy on the floor.'
Interviewer: 'Then what happened?'

Interviewer: 'Why did you get the gun?'
Robbie: 'So he would stop hitting Mommy.'
Interviewer: 'Did you know the gun would hurt him?'
Robbie: 'Yes. It makes a bang and he stopped.'
Interviewer: 'Are you afraid of anything now?'
Robbie: 'No. He can't hit her anymore.'

De Becker's framework explains both the event and the disbelief: child abuse is the single most reliable pre-incident indicator of family killing, and children under abuse behave with the same docility as adult victims of rape or hijacking, so their competence and their silence tell us nothing against them. Robbie's chilling clarity is the voice of a child who has been living with violence all his short life; the gun report laid the family's secrets bare, and the answer to 'how could he?' lies in the years of beatings, not in the boy.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: Evidence vs. verdict: (1) Sequence evidence: the account places the shooting seconds after a witnessed beating, consistent with the mother's recorded injuries and the father's drinking that night. (2) Physical evidence: gunpowder tests confirmed Robbie fired the weapon, resolving the 'impossible' objection, and the same objection would have had force against any abused child witness and none. (3) Motive evidence: Robbie's recorded explanations are exclusively protective ('so he would stop hitting Mommy'), matching Mones's finding that abused children who kill are acting out of years of beatings and degradation and that the report of the gun 'lays family secrets bare.' (4) Docility norm: adults who doubt Robbie's competence to act or report are applying a standard no one applies to adult victims of rape or hijacking, who are equally docile and never blamed. Verdict: the act and the account are the terminal expression of documented family abuse; the reliable PIN was the father's violence, and the intervention that failed was the protection of the mother and child, not the child's disposition.

The mother manipulated Robbie into shooting her husband so that she could avoid prosecution.

assets.topic: The principal's assurance audit: 'We could not have predicted'
assets.visual_frame_description: A principal's office with two framed district awards on the wall above a dark wooden desk. Principal Dale Hargrove, a 22-year district veteran, sits across from investigators who have placed a transfer file, an arrest report, and a policy manual titled 'Child-On-Child Sexual Abuse' on the desk between them. A security camera feed on the wall monitor shows the playground, where a 9-year-old walks beside a slightly older student escort.
assets.player_mission: Audit the principal's statement that the assault could not have been predicted against the documents in front of him. Determine whether his assurance is accurate, self-protective spin, or active suppression of known indicators.
key_concepts: Schools are in the business of high-stakes predictions, including whether a student will sexually abuse another child or bring a lethal weapon to school.

The school district in the Joey case had a specific written policy titled 'Child-On-Child Sexual Abuse,' which de Becker notes makes clear such things happen and raises a predictive question for every principal.
Joey had been arrested a month earlier for victimizing another boy in the same way in the same bathroom.
Joey's previous school predicted in writing that he would act out in sexually inappropriate ways and sent his records to the school where the offenses occurred.
The principal did not tell Joey's teachers about the first accusation, so no increase in supervision was possible.
When Joey was found unmanageable, he was moved to a class of younger, smaller boys, a virtual 'beauty contest' of victims.
The principal arranged for Joey to be escorted to the bathroom by another student rather than by a teacher or guard.
Security guards at that school received no training, guidelines, post instructions, or policies about student safety, and were not told even to 'be extra alert.'
Untrained guards can hurt more than help because, having taken the expensive step of hiring them, everyone stops looking at safety and security.
De Becker attributes such failures to organizational and individual laziness and the hope that something will 'go away' if ignored.
assets.theory_summary: This audit tests feigned ignorance versus documented knowledge in institutional settings: the claim 'could not have been predicted' collides with written predictions, a formal abuse policy, and a prior arrest in the same bathroom. De Becker's diagnosis is that the school possessed the information and declined the response, because prediction without preparation is merely curiosity, and institutions prefer the comfort of hiring guards to the work of supervision.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.question: Was Principal Hargrove's statement that the assault 'could not have been predicted' truthful?
assets.subject_baseline: Hargrove is a 22-year district employee with a reputation among staff for being affable and procedurally cautious. Teacher evaluations note he 'runs a tight ship' on attendance records and keys. In prior meetings about Joey's first accusation, he described himself as 'a manager, not a therapist,' and told teachers to keep the matter confidential. He chairs the campus safety committee, which has met six times in two years without producing a written procedure.
assets.observed_nonverbal_log: 14:02 Audit opens; Hargrove enters carrying a coffee mug labeled 'SAFETY FIRST' and sits with his hands flat on the desk. 14:11 When the transfer file is placed in front of him, he pushes it two inches away without opening it while saying 'I was never given that.' 14:19 Asked about the prior-school prediction, he stares at the ceiling for five seconds and answers 'If such a letter existed, I would have acted.' 14:27 Told the letter is stamped received in his office's log, he rotates the mug slowly and says 'I have three thousand students and fifty things on my desk.' 14:36 Asked about the student escort arrangement, he describes it as 'a privilege for our older students to help,' and his voice drops to a near-warm register. 14:47 Asked about the 'Child-On-Child Sexual Abuse' policy, he says 'sure, it's in the manual' and flips several pages, smiling, without reading the relevant heading. 14:55 The investigator reads the arrest report aloud; Hargrove stops smiling, breathes out slowly, and says 'The summer paperwork is a mess.'
assets.interrogation_transcript:
Investigator: 'Sir, did you know a month before this offense that this student had been arrested for assaulting a boy the same way in the same bathroom?'
Hargrove: 'If I had, of course I would have increased supervision. We can't act on what we don't know.'
Investigator: 'The prior school sent a written prediction with his records.'
Hargrove: 'I have three thousand students. These letters arrive by the box.'
Investigator: 'Your office log shows it was received and initialed by your assistant.'
Hargrove: 'The summer paperwork is a mess.'
Investigator: 'Why was he moved into the younger children's class?'
Hargrove: 'He was disruptive in fourth grade. The younger class has a calmer teacher.'
Investigator: 'And the student who escorts him to the bathroom?'
Hargrove: 'Our older students enjoy helping. It builds character.'
Investigator: 'Were your security guards told anything about this student?'
Hargrove: 'Guards are for deterrence. I don't brief them on individual children.'
assets.correct_diagnosis: The assurance is not truthful: it is institutional denial with a veneer of proceduralism. The record contradicts the claim element by element: a written prediction from the prior school was logged into the office, an arrest for the identical offense in the identical bathroom preceded the assault by a month, and the district's own 'Child-On-Child Sexual Abuse' policy had existed for years, meaning the risk class was officially foreseeable. Hargrove's responses show the 'we could not have predicted' defense resting entirely on not reading documents he signed for, an escort arrangement that placed victims beside the offender, and guards trained and briefed on nothing. De Becker's diagnosis covers the pattern precisely: organizations under pressure hire guards so everyone can feel the matter addressed, but untrained, unbriefed presence can hurt more than help because the expensive step ends scrutiny; and the hope that the problem would 'go away' if ignored is itself a described failure mode. The truthful statement is the opposite of his: the school predicted in writing, and declined to act.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: Evidence vs. verdict: (1) Receipt evidence: the office log proves the written prediction arrived and was initialed, defeating the 'never given that' defense, and de Becker's Joey case shows the same letter system failing the same way. (2) Recency evidence: a one-month-old arrest for the identical offense in the identical bathroom is the strongest possible short-window PIN, making the 'couldn't have known' claim untenable without the deliberate act of not reading. (3) Policy evidence: a standing 'Child-On-Child Sexual Abuse' policy demonstrates official knowledge that such offenses happen and obliges principals to answer the predictive question 'who might this be,' which de Becker frames as Joey standing up in the imaginary assembly while the principal turned away. (4) Response evidence: failing to inform teachers, moving the offender into a class of younger and smaller children, and assigning a student escort are not neutral acts; each transmits risk onto other children. (5) Security evidence: untrained, unbriefed guards are comfort theater, and de Becker warns that taking the expensive step makes everyone stop looking at safety. Verdict: deceptive assurance; the knowledge was in the building and the actions maximized rather than reduced exposure.
distractors: The principal acted reasonably on the information available and the district's lawyers correctly advised that his statements are accurate.
The claim is partially true because a nine-year-old's future behavior is legally unpredictable regardless of documented history.
The principal's responsibility ended with referring the matter to the security guards, whose professional judgment was his to rely on.

assets.topic: James Vance's self-explanation audit: blaming the band
assets.visual_frame_description: A cold deposition room where two cameras record from opposite corners. Eighteen-year-old James Vance, chin gone decades of reconstruction into a towel-wrapped mask, sits with his mother beside him; a q-and-a lawyer holds a lyric sheet. Photographs of a sawed-off shotgun and a churchyard lie in a clear sleeve on the table, and the room hums with the fluorescent light overhead.
assets.player_mission: Audit James's own account of the shootings and determine whether his attribution to the band survives contact with his other statements. Separate the lyric argument from the pre-incident indicators present in his own narrative.
key_concepts: James Vance was obsessed with Judas Priest and their violent public persona, calling the band 'metal gods' who were 'his bible.'
Of his relationship with band members he never met, he said it was 'like a marriage—intimacy that developed over a period of time, and it was until death do us part.'
Asked about the lyric 'they bathed him and clothed him and fed him by hand,' he recited it as 'they bathed him and clothed him and fed him a hand,' having rewritten a caring image into cannibalism.
He said he would do anything for the band, 'kill many people or shoot the president through the head.'
He said that if the band had declared a contest to kill the most people, he would have gone out and done something terrible, though the band said no such thing.
He planned to become a gunsmith and played 'war' games as 'training to be a mercenary,' boasting he outdrew both cops in his games ninety-nine percent of the time.
He said of watching television, 'just watching TV, you learn. TV is a really good teacher.'
He admitted 'Violence excited me' and that he felt 'ignored for 20 years.'
He and Ray were high on drugs and alcohol on the night of the shootings and had considered a shooting spree at a shopping center.
By pointing at the band, James washed away the scrutiny that might reasonably have been focused on himself, his family, or his society.
assets.theory_summary: This audit tests the causal story a perpetrator offers against the causal evidence he supplies elsewhere: James's account blames lyrics, while his own statements document fascination with guns, war games, substance use, excitement about violence, and twenty years of felt invisibility. De Becker's verdict is that the media were a stage, not a script, and the attribution to the band functioned to shield the more uncomfortable causes from scrutiny.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.question: Does James Vance's own account support the claim that the album caused his and Ray's suicide pact and shootings?
assets.subject_baseline: James is articulate, patient under questioning, and cooperative with lawyers, aided by his mother who interprets his damaged speech. He describes the band with organized devotion and keeps returning to album lyrics as causes. His account of family life is thin; when asked about his parents, he offers that he was 'ignored for 20 years' and then returns to the music.

The stars being right? The tide being out? No.'
assets.interrogation_transcript:
Counsel: 'Why did you and Ray do what you did?'
Vance: 'The music. We were devoted. It was like a marriage with the band, until death do us part.'
Counsel: 'Did the band tell you to do it?'
Vance: 'They didn't have to. If they said, let's see who can kill the most people, I would have gone out and done something terrible.'
Counsel: 'You've been drinking and using drugs that night?'
Vance: 'Everybody was. An alcoholic is a very violent individual, and when you drink excessively, you become violent, and that has been my life experience.'
Counsel: 'What about guns?'
Vance: 'I was going to be a gunsmith. We went shooting all the time. Watching TV, you learn. TV is a really good teacher.'
Counsel: 'Did you want to hurt anyone?'
Vance: 'Violence excited me.'
Counsel: 'Anything else that might explain it?'
Vance: 'A bad relationship? The stars being right? The tide being out? No.'
assets.correct_diagnosis: The attribution to the album does not withstand James's own account; it is an external attribution masking the PINs present in his narrative. In a single deposition he supplies the leading indicators: an obsession with guns including a gunsmith plan and regular target shooting; 'war' games played as mercenary training in which he routinely outdrew pretend officers; heavy drinking and drug use on the night, which he connects to violence from his own experience; the admission that 'violence excited me'; and the 'ignored for 20 years' statement de Becker calls one of the leading PINs for attention-getting violent acts. His lyric argument fails on its own evidence: he did not merely receive the songs, he rewrote them (turning 'fed him by hand' into 'fed him a hand'), and he asserted the band need not command him because his own readiness was complete. The court's real-world conclusion matched the audit: the proprietors could not have predicted the shootings, because the causes were in the boy's own history, not in the album.
assets.diagnostic_breakdown: Evidence vs. verdict: (1) Rewriting evidence: James altered 'fed him by hand' to 'fed him a hand,' transforming nurturance into cannibalism, which demonstrates the violence was pre-existing and shaping the media, not the reverse. (2) Readiness evidence: his statement that he would have committed murder on the band's word, though the band never spoke, removes the music from the causal chain and leaves his own disposition. (3) PIN evidence: gunsmith ambitions, war-play training, substance use ('that goes hand in hand,' 'alcoholics are violent'), excitement over violence, and twenty years of felt invisibility are each on de Becker's list of the hundred influences, and alcohol and drugs sit closer to the top than media addiction. (4) Attribution evidence: his sarcastic catalogue 'a bad relationship? The stars being right? The tide being out?' shows his causal standard collapses once family life is excluded, and blaming the band functioned precisely to wash away scrutiny of himself, his family, and his society. Verdict: the explanation is the offender's own narrative redirection; the pre-incident indicators he described in his own words carried the predictive weight.

James minimized the band's influence to protect himself from prosecution for copying their violent fantasy.
The record producer's subliminal engineering of the album's percussion tracks is the actual mechanism behind the suicide pact.

assets.topic: The denial boss: 'He's just a typical teenager'
assets.visual_frame_description: The living room of the Ortega family home in San Antonio on a Friday night. Fifteen-year-old Mateo is on the couch beside his uncle Rafael, and his mother Elena is at the dining table folding laundry. On the TV, a video game shows a shooting scene, and Mateo is reenacting it enthusiastically while his uncle laughs; empty beer bottles glint on the side table next to Mateo's stack of band magazines featuring violent album art.
assets.player_mission: Defeat the boss named Denial by reading the scene correctly and then choosing the intervention that changes Mateo's trajectory. The boss attacks by labelling every indicator 'normal teenage behavior,' and you must prove otherwise and act.
key_concepts: Warning signs for teen violence are usually plentiful, as with Jason Massey, whose cruelty to animals, idolization of killers, robbery, and five-year stalking of a girl were all known before he killed, 'and yet denial prevailed.'
De Becker's hypothetical list of the hundred most significant influences puts alcohol and drugs near the top, above addiction to media products.
A fascination with violence and guns is a central PIN, and James Vance's gun obsession extended to planning to become a gunsmith and playing 'war' as training for combat.
James said 'violence excited me' and felt 'ignored for 20 years,' which de Becker identifies as a leading PIN for attention-getting violent acts.
Daniel Goleman lists seven abilities beneficial for humans, including empathy and impulse control; many who commit violence never learned them, and chronic anger in childhood is another predictor.
77 percent of homicides by young people occur when they are high or drunk, so substance use during encounters with violent youth is the most dangerous context.
Media content matters, but the amount matters more: consumption that replaces human interaction is the bigger issue, whether the music is rock, heavy metal, or classical.

David Walsh compares the violence children witness in media to 'a guest in our families that advocates violence,' noting children learn by modeling and imitation of the 200,000 acts of violence they will witness by age 18.
Ressler and Alice Miller argue that kindness, support, or interest from an adult during the critical early puberty years can turn potential offenders around; 'it doesn't take much.'
When a child's primary caregiver delivers both praise and brutality, it is a virtual coin toss as to which will attach itself to the child's identity.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests the victory condition of accurate PIN recognition over the boss of minimization: the scene is a stockpile of documented indicators wearing ordinary-family clothing, and denial's signature move is renaming each one 'a phase.' De Becker's evidence, from Massey's known and ignored warning signs to the PIN list built from the Vance case, is that the indicators are present and countable before violence, so the losing move is to wait for the outcome.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.stage_1_observation: Watch the Ortega living room and catalogue the indicators visible in one evening: Mateo's excited reenactment of on-screen shootings, the empty beer bottles within his reach, his stack of violent album art, and his later remark to his uncle that nobody at school even knows he exists. Notice that Elena says nothing about the bottles and Rafael frames the reenactment as 'boys being boys.'
assets.stage_1_question: Which combination of details is the strongest warning-sign cluster in this scene?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: The cluster of substance use (beer within reach), excited engagement with violence rather than ordinary viewing ('violence excited me' pattern), and the felt-invisibility statement are the documented PINs that matter; the album covers and video game are the camouflage that the Denial boss will point to as causes or as normal taste. De Becker's PIN list ranks alcohol and drugs near the top, a fascination with violence high, and chronic felt invisibility among the leading indicators for attention-getting acts, while Goleman's missing abilities and chronic anger mark the boy who needs help.
assets.stage_2_intervention: Elena must choose Mateo's next step after she confirms the bottle and hears the invisibility remark. Options: (a) confiscate the video games and albums and forbid the music outright; (b) buy Mateo more of the band's albums to connect with his interest and talk about the artwork; (c) sit down with Mateo, acknowledge his feelings of being unseen, and arrange counseling and supervised social activity while removing easy access to alcohol; (d) say nothing now and increase his allowance so he can afford his own things and stop feeling left out.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Option (c): engage the boy as a human being and change the environment. De Becker's evidence weighs the amount of media consumption and the human interaction it replaces more than the specific content, and Ressler and Miller document that kindness, support, or simple interest from an adult during the critical early-puberty period can turn a potential offender around; de Becker adds that 'it doesn't take much' and that a child's self-worth reflected in an encouraging adult's attention is worth more than any confiscation. Confiscation (a) treats content as the cause the book's evidence rejects, buying more of the albums (b) treats the obsession as nurture rather than signal, and silence with money (d) is the Denial boss's own move, since it leaves the substance access, the excitement pattern, and the invisibility untouched.
assets.boss_battle_explanation: The boss of this battle is the denial reflex: adults bend the facts of a child's escalating, obsessive behavior until they fit the reassuring story that 'he is just a typical teenager.' de Becker shows how this minimization of warning signs, driven by discomfort and the wish to see the best, is what allowed the case in the chapter to progress to its tragic end; the correct move is to trust the record of escalating behavior over the comforting label.

assets.topic: The school-safety boss: high-stakes prediction vs. comfort
assets.visual_frame_description: Back-to-school night at Westbrook Elementary in Oregon. In the gymnasium, Principal Vaughn presents a slideshow titled 'Safety Comes First' while two security guards stand by the doors, untrained in anything written down and chatting with each other about their shift schedules. At the edge of the crowd, a parent named Priya Sharma watches a younger student being escorted down the hall by a slightly older student while a banner above reads 'Every Child Welcomed.'
assets.player_mission: Defeat the boss named Comfort by seeing through the security theater on display. Your decisions determine whether a documented warning-sign file in a sibling school's records gets acted on or buried, and whether your own child's safety is a promise or a prediction.
key_concepts: Schools are in the business of high-stakes predictions, facing questions such as whether a visitor will kidnap a child, whether a teacher will molest a child, whether a child is being abused at home, or whether a student will bring a lethal weapon to school.
Hiring guards is the typical response when organizations are pressured to improve security, and everyone sighs and feels the matter has been addressed.
Guards who are not trained or supervised or properly equipped, with no intelligent plan to follow, can hurt more than help because everyone stops looking at safety and security.

In the Joey case, security guards at the school received no training on any aspect of student safety, no written guidelines, no post instructions, and were not told even 'be extra alert' or 'keep an eye out.'
The principal in the Joey case ordered the dangerous boy escorted by another student rather than by a teacher or guard.
The school district's policy book did not raise student safety until page 10, and that reference was about faculty safety when breaking up fights; danger to students appeared only on page 91.
The policy book devoted three full pages and twenty-one separate items to the protection of keys.
Federal law requires colleges to maintain campus crime statistics and provide them upon request, but no similar law requires grammar schools or high schools to keep such statistics.
Just the fact that parents ask puts safety on the agenda and forces the school to focus on it.

Parents should request a copy of the school's safety policies, ask about background screening for employees, ask to meet security personnel and probe their training, and ask about previous crimes at the school.
assets.theory_summary: This battle tests outcomes-based safety reasoning against the purchasing of comfort: institutions spend on visible symbols like guards precisely so that scrutiny stops, and de Becker's school cases show the spent step substitutes for the unperformed one. The victory condition is making the high-stakes prediction visible again by asking the obvious questions that force policy into the open.

credibility.basis: Observational case-based expertise (de Becker's violence-prevention practice)

assets.stage_1_observation: Study the back-to-school-night scene: the two guards with no paperwork anywhere in sight, the principal's slideshow with no mention of background screening or incident statistics, the student-to-student escort in the hallway, and the district policy handbook resting on a table where a quick peek reveals the word 'students' first appears near the end of the book. Note also that Priya overhears a teacher say that Joey's file 'followed him' from the other school.
assets.stage_1_question: Which detail is the most meaningful indicator that safety at this school is not actually being addressed?
assets.stage_1_correct_answer: The guards' complete lack of training, written guidelines, post instructions, or briefing on student-safety topics, combined with the student escorting another student arrangement, is the meaningful indicator: it reproduces the Joey-case pattern where a trained human resource was never engaged, and an untrained presence 'can hurt more than help because everyone stops looking at safety and security.' The presence of guards alone is the comfort purchase de Becker diagnoses; the actual safety function requires supervision, information, and an intelligent plan, none of which is visible, while the policy book that buries student danger on page 91 confirms safety is not on the operational agenda.
assets.stage_2_intervention: Priya must decide how to force the issue at school. Options: (a) thank the principal for the visible security presence and enroll her daughter normally; (b) hire a private guard to shadow her daughter at playground hours at her own expense; (c) request the district's safety policy document, ask about background screening for employees, ask to meet the guards and probe what they were trained on, and ask about previous crimes at the school; (d) transfer her daughter to the nearby private academy without asking any questions.
assets.stage_2_correct_answer: Option (c): send the written request and ask the obvious questions in person. De Becker's parental strategy is explicit: request the school's safety policies, ask about background screening, meet security personnel and see how they respond to probing questions, and ask about previous crimes, because 'just the fact that you ask puts safety on the agenda and forces the school to focus on it' and because no federal law compels elementary schools to publish crime statistics as colleges must, so the demand must come from parents. Thanking the school (a) rewards the comfort purchase, hiring a private guard (b) repeats the untrained-presence error in miniature, and fleeing to another school (d) leaves the predictive question unanswered for every other child in the building.
assets.boss_battle_explanation: The boss of this battle is the pressure to promise safety instead of predicting danger: school officials facing a credible threat prefer the comforting assertion that 'we could not have predicted this' because it absolves them in advance. de Becker's counterclaim is that warning signs were present and identifiable, so the winning strategy is to take the threat seriously, escalate protection, and prefer action over reassurance even when the prediction risks being wrong.
